title: The Fox Without a Tail
text:
A fox was caught in a trap. He struggled and twisted and finally tore himself free, but he left his fine bushy tail behind in the iron jaws. When he limped home, he realized how ridiculous he looked, and he dreaded the laughter of the other foxes.

So he made a plan. He called all the foxes to a meeting and gave a serious speech. Tails, he told them, were a nuisance. They were heavy, they dragged in the mud, they got caught in brambles, and they gave hounds something to grab. He had lately tried living without one, and he could honestly say he had never felt lighter or freer. He urged them all to cut off their tails at once.

The foxes listened politely. Then an old fox at the back spoke up. If you still had your own tail, he said, I doubt you would be giving us this advice. The meeting ended in laughter, and every fox kept its tail.
lesson: When someone urges the whole group to adopt a change, ask what that person gains from it. Advice that would spread someone's own loss to everyone deserves a second look.
source: Aesop's Fables, The Fox Who Had Lost His Tail
